one_liner: Pure-Rust block compressor using 4-byte hashed dictionary units; compresses faster than LZ4 at matching ratios, decompresses slower.
what_it_does: Density is a raw in-memory buffer compressor (crate density-rs, formerly a C99 library) with three algorithms: Chameleon (fastest), Cheetah (middle) and Lion (best ratio). The Rust API is Chameleon::encode(&input, &mut output) / Chameleon::decode(...) returning Result<usize, _>, with safe_encode_buffer_size() for sizing the output; since 0.16.6 each algorithm also exports extern "C" functions (chameleon_encode, chameleon_decode, chameleon_safe_encode_buffer_size, and the cheetah/lion equivalents). There is no frame or container format: the stream carries no original length or checksum, so the caller must store the decompressed size.
how_it_is_fast: It is not an LZ77 matcher: input is read 16 bytes at a time as a u128 and split into four 32-bit 'quads'; each quad is hashed (multiply by 0x9D6EF916, keep the top 16 bits) into a 64K-entry u32 dictionary, and a hit emits a 2-byte hash index while a miss emits the 4 literal bytes, with 1 flag bit per quad packed into a 64-bit signature word. Cheetah adds a second dictionary slot and a predictor, Lion five predictors. There is no match search, no variable-length offsets and no entropy coder, and a 'blowup protection' state machine switches blocks to plain copy when two consecutive blocks fail to shrink.
when_to_use: Compression throughput is the bottleneck and decode volume is similar or lower, e.g. write-heavy logging, snapshotting or spill-to-disk where data is written once and read rarely.
Large text-like or moderately redundant buffers (tens of MB), where the 4-byte dictionary has time to learn; Cheetah (-2) matches LZ4-default ratio while compressing about 1.4x faster in lzbench 2.4.
Rust codebases wanting a dependency-free, bounds-checked codec with no unsafe code on the data path, or C/C++ code willing to link a Rust staticlib through the 0.16.6 C functions.
Incompressible or mixed inputs, where the copy-mode protection keeps output at most 8 bytes per 256-byte block above the input size.
when_not_to_use: Read-heavy workloads: decompression is 1617 MB/s for Chameleon versus 3832-3977 MB/s for LZ4 on the same lzbench table, so LZ4, LZSSE or ZXC decode 2.4x or more faster.
When interoperability matters: the format is not standardised, has no framing, length header or checksum, and changed across the C-to-Rust rewrite (0.14.x C streams are a different codebase).
Small messages: the README says the algorithms 'are less performant on very small datasets' because the 4-byte dictionary learns slowly.

Untrusted or corrupted input from C/C++: decode never returns an error; malformed data or a too-small output buffer hits a Rust slice bounds check and panics, which through the extern "C" functions aborts the process (Rust 1.81+ behavior).
If you only need one fast-compress point: memlz 0.5 beta in the same lzbench table compresses at 4452 MB/s at 59.90% size, faster and smaller than Density -1 (1630 MB/s, 62.77%).

integration.form: crate (Rust); C callers must build it as a staticlib/cdylib themselves (no header or C build files shipped)
integration.dependencies: none at runtime (dev-dependencies divan, snap, lz4_flex for benches only)
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.85 (edition 2024); lzbench's wrapper crate states 1.85 as Density's minimum
integration.platforms: any Rust target; CI tests x86-64 Linux/macOS/Windows (MSVC and GNU), i686, aarch64, and big-endian powerpc64 and s390x; no SIMD or arch-specific code
integration.thread_safety: not documented; each encode/decode call allocates its own 256 KiB dictionary state, so separate calls on separate threads share nothing

gotchas: Errors are effectively panics: encode and decode always return Ok, and all bounds problems surface as slice-index panics; the C wrappers return 0 only for an Err that never occurs.
Every static encode/decode call allocates and zeroes a 64K-entry u32 table (256 KiB); reuse a Chameleon::new() instance for many small buffers, or the setup dominates.
The level-to-algorithm mapping in lzbench is -1 Chameleon, -2 Cheetah, -3 Lion; Lion compresses at only 442 MB/s with 578 MB/s decode, slower than LZ4 default on both sides.

lzbench documents earlier bugs: its README carried a warning about density 0.14.2 producing shortened decompressed output (issues #92 and #94 asked about it and were closed without a written answer); fuzzing crashes (#60) and an encoder division by zero (#56) were fixed in the C era.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Density over LZ4 or Snappy when compression speed matters more than decode speed: Cheetah gives LZ4-default ratio at 1.4x LZ4's compression speed, and Chameleon gives LZ4 --fast -17 ratio at 1.8x its speed. For fast decode pick LZ4, ZXC or LZSSE; for the fastest compress-only point at this ratio memlz is ahead.
verified_claims_summary: In lzbench 2.4 (gcc 15.2.0 release binary, density built with cargo inside lzbench, one thread of an AMD EPYC 9555P with turbo off, silesia.tar), Density 0.16.6 -1 compresses at 1630 MB/s to 62.77% versus LZ4 1.10.0 --fast -17 at 924 MB/s and 62.15% (about 1.8x), and -2 at 767 MB/s to 47.94% versus LZ4 default at 550 MB/s and 47.60% (about 1.4x, derived from page data); decompression is 758-1617 MB/s versus LZ4's 3832-3977 MB/s. The repo's own cargo bench compares only against the Rust ports lz4_flex and snap, not the C libraries.
status_note: Last commit and crate release 0.16.6 on 2025-08-27 (C bindings added), zero open issues, about 1k stars and 6.6k crate downloads; small, MIT OR Apache-2.0, and easy to vendor, but effectively single-maintainer and quiet for 13 months.
